prompt_text:
The figure summarizes B-cell development and several key functions of mature B cells. At the top, it shows a progression from stem cells in the bone marrow through pro-B, pre-B, immature, and transitional B cells, then into naïve B cells that circulate in secondary lymphoid organs and can differentiate into memory B cells, plasmablasts, and antibody-secreting plasma cells. A bar chart beneath this pathway compares how surface markers change across stages, indicating that different markers and antibody isotypes appear or disappear as B cells mature.

The lower panels highlight major immune roles of activated B cells. One panel depicts class switching driven by help from a T follicular helper cell, with signals such as IL-21 and factors including BCL-6 and CXCR5 leading to production of a different antibody class. Another shows antibody production by plasmablasts or plasma cells, with antibodies acting through complement, direct cell killing, or NK-cell-mediated mechanisms like ADCC/ADCP to eliminate target cells. Additional panels show antigen presentation, where a B cell internalizes antigen through the B-cell receptor and presents peptide on MHC to a T cell, and cytokine production, where distinct B-cell subsets appear to promote either inflammatory or regulatory T-cell responses.
